consensus_summary: Primary symbolic sense of 'Jew' is the true/inward covenant member whose heart is circumcised by the Spirit (not mere ethnic/outward identity), with etymological link to Judah/praise; the term also retains ordinary ethnic/religious sense, context deciding, while false claimants appear in Rev; no single settled consensus exists beyond the shared Pauline texts.
book_summary: In covenant contexts, a Jew is one in the covenant inwardly ('he is a Jew, which is one inwardly'), while some claim the name falsely; the name derives from Judah meaning praise so that the inward Jew is one whose praise is of God; the word also functions plainly as ethnic/religious, context deciding which sense applies.
consensus_core_identification: inward/true covenant member (heart circumcision by Spirit, praise of God) as opposed to merely outward/ethnic; dual plain ethnic sense; false claimants
book_core_identification: one in the covenant inwardly (with praise-of-God etymology) versus false claimants; dual plain ethnic/religious sense decided by context
boundary_disagreement: none; both treat the inward-covenant sense as the principal symbolic use while retaining the ordinary ethnic sense without redefining its scope
rationale: Minimum cores are identical: both identify the primary symbolic referent as the inward covenant member of Romans 2:28-29 whose identity is confirmed by the Judah/praise etymology, both acknowledge false claimants (Rev 3:9), and both insist the term also walks in plain ethnic/religious dress with context deciding. Differences are only wording and degree of elaboration on alternatives; no replacement of referent, no narrowing/broadening of cases, and no contradiction.
strongest_objection: The book's brevity omits explicit discussion of supersessionist or dispensational extensions that some consensus responses flag as contested alternatives, but this does not alter the shared core identification.
